newsitem.title: INDIA: India's RBI puts credit controls on wheat buying.
newsitem.headline: India's RBI puts credit controls on wheat buying.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Tuesday put wheat back under selective credit control for three months in response to domestic price rises and falling availability, the Press Trust of India (PTI) reported.

The minimum margins and level of credit ceiling on advances against wheat stocks for mills and processing units would be 45 percent, the news agency said. For others like traders it would be 60 percent and against warehouse receipts 45 percent.

The RBI said all other rules in force prior to the removal of selective credit controls on advances against wheat in October 1993, would be reactivated. Controls were eased in 1993 after a bumper crop.
The RBI uses selective credit controls to discourage traders from using bank funds to hoard essential commodities.

Analysts say that together with the restriction on credit, traders would be discouraged from funding wheat purchases and more wheat would be available in the market. The move would also help the government's own procurement operations.
The RBI in Bombay was closed on Tuesday for a holiday in the western state of Maharastra.

Early this month the government agreed to pay a bonus of 600 rupees per tonne to farmers in addition to the 4,150 rupee purchase price. The bonus will be payable on wheat offered for sale to procurement agencies for the central pool up to June 10, 1997.

Farmers in the states of Punjab and Haryana, which contribute 80 percent of India's wheat output, have been agitating for higher prices, seeking parity with prices at which the government imports wheat.
Bhupinder Singh Mann, president of the farmers organisation Bharatiya Kisan Union (BKU), said the government was paying $180 a tonne for imported wheat.
India has signed contracts to import 2.7 million tonnes of wheat since December 1996. --Bombay Newsroom, (91) 22 265 9000
